steps.body: Your ×2 machine has a turbo button. **×4 = double twice**: two 2s make a 4. **×8 = double three times**: three doublings stack up to 8. Every ×4 and ×8 fact is just your doubles, run again.
Watch ×4 get built from two doublings.

panels.title: Double once
panels.body: 7 doubled is 14. That's 7 × 2 — two groups of 7.

panels.title: Double again
panels.body: 14 doubled is 28. Doubling the two groups makes FOUR groups: 7 × 4 = 28.

panels.title: Why it works
panels.body: Two, doubled, is four — so doubling a ×2 answer turns it into the ×4 answer. Your doubles carry you to facts you never memorized.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep revealing — the second doubling lands next.
widget.successFeedback: 7 → 14 → 28. Double-double turns any ×2 skill into ×4 power.

explanationVariants: Double 6 to get 12, double again to get 24: 6 × 4 = 24.

commonErrors.feedback: 10 adds 6 + 4. The 4 says take four 6s — or faster: double 6, then double again.
12 is one doubling — that's 6 × 2. To reach ×4, double AGAIN: 12 + 12.
18 adds one more 6 after the first doubling — that's 6 × 3. The double-double doubles the whole 12.

steps.body: ×8 just adds one more doubling. 3 × 8: double 3 → 6, double → 12, double → 24. **Count your doublings** — one for ×2, two for ×4, three for ×8. Lose count and you land on the wrong fact.

widget.prompt: Start at 5 and double exactly three times. Enter the final number in the doubling chain.

commonErrors.feedback: 13 adds 5 + 8. Eight 5s stack much higher — run three doublings: 10, 20, 40.
20 is two doublings — that's 5 × 4. ×8 needs one MORE doubling: 20 + 20.
58 glues the digits together. Double your way there instead: 5 → 10 → 20 → 40.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count three doublings on your fingers: 5 → 10 → 20 → ?

steps.body: Build the array reached after three doublings.

widget.prompt: Start with 3 × 4, then double the number of columns. Build the 3-by-8 array.
widget.factorFeedback: Use side lengths 3 and 8. The lesson is tracking how three doublings make 8 copies of 3.
widget.lowFeedback: The array has fewer than 24 squares. Double the 4-copy side to 8.
widget.highFeedback: The array has more than 24 squares. Use exactly 3 rows and 8 columns, or turn that array.
widget.successFeedback: The 3-by-8 array has 24 squares. Doubling 3 three times makes 3 × 8: 3 → 6 → 12 → 24.

predict.prompt: Doubling 3 three times (3 → 6 → 12 → 24) is the same as multiplying 3 by…
predict.reveal: Double, double, double is ×2 · ×2 · ×2 = ×8 — so 3 × 8 = 24 without ever knowing your 8s. Doubling just twice is the same trick for ×4.

steps.body: Each doubling **moves you to a new fact** — know which one.
explanationVariants: Doubling a ×2 fact lands on the ×4 fact: 18 doubled is 36, so 9 × 4 = 36.

widget.prompt: Lena knows 9 × 2 = 18. If she doubles that answer ONCE more, which fact does she get?

options.feedback: Doubling the two groups makes four groups: 9 × 4 = 36.
×3 needs ADDING one more 9 (18 + 9), not doubling. Doubling jumps straight from ×2 to ×4.
×8 takes doubling TWICE more from here. One more doubling only reaches ×4.
Doubling changes which fact you're on — 9 × 2 stays 18. The new answer, 36, belongs to 9 × 4.

hints: 6 spiders × 8 legs is a ×8 fact — run the doubling machine starting from 6.
6 → 12 → 24 — that's two doublings. ×8 needs one more.

widget.prompt: A spider has 8 legs. How many legs do 6 spiders have in all?

commonErrors.feedback: 14 adds 6 + 8. Six spiders each bring 8 whole legs — double 6 three times instead.
24 is two doublings — that's 6 × 4, a four-legged spider! One more doubling reaches ×8.
96 doubled one time too many — that's 6 × 16. Count exactly three doublings for ×8: 12, 24, 48.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Run the chain from 6 and stop after the third doubling: 6 → 12 → 24 → ?

takeaways: Count your doublings — each one moves you to a new fact.
Doubling a known answer (like 9 × 2) unlocks the next fact free.
steps.teaser: the nines hide the prettiest pattern in the whole times table.

concept.body: Quick rewind. ×4 is just **double, then double again**. Try 2 × 4: double 2 is 4, double 4 is 8 — so 2 × 4 = 8. Whisper the chain as you go: it's one doubling for ×2, two for ×4.

explanationVariants: Double 4 to get 8, double 8 to get 16: 4 × 4 = 16.

options.feedback: 4 → 8 → 16: double twice and you've got it.
8 is one doubling — that's 4 × 2. Double again for ×4.
12 adds one more 4 after the first doubling — that's 4 × 3. Double the whole 8 instead: 8 + 8.
